meta.notes: Each question supports two views. The default view explains why the key is correct: 'takeaway' is the clinical rule and each option carries its own rationale. The strategy view uses 'elimination', which names the test-taking strategies in play, walks the options out one at a time, and ends with the verdict. Both views describe the same question, so a student who is short on content can still reason to the answer. All fields are plain text with no markup, so render 'strategy' in italic with CSS rather than expecting tags. Every chapter and skills section carries an 'exam' field naming the exam it belongs to; meta.exams lists the sections in each. Filter on 'exam' to build a single exam's bank. The top-level 'chapters' and 'skills' arrays stay flat and hold every exam, so anything reading them without filtering still sees the whole course. Chapters carry both 'id' (unique key) and 'chapterNumber' (the number to display); they match except for The Endocrine System and Diabetes Mellitus, which displays as 56 and uses id 1056 because two different chapters in this course are numbered 56. Daily sets: questions written for a given day carry a 'dailySet' field holding that date (YYYY-MM-DD). Only one daily set exists at a time — generating a new one strips 'dailySet' from every question that has it, then applies it to the new batch. meta.currentDailySet mirrors the active date and ids. Filter on the presence of 'dailySet' to pull today's set; questions keep their chapter membership and stay in the bank permanently after the tag is removed. 'source' is Potter or Iggy. Chapter numbers repeat across the two books, so 'id' is the unique key: Potter chapters use id = chapter number, Iggy chapters use id = 1000 + chapter number. Question ids are prefixed ch<n>- for Potter and ig<n>- for Iggy. Display chapterNumber with source, never id.

questionTypes.multiple_choice: one correct option; answer is a string
questionTypes.sata: select all that apply; answer is an array and is scored all or nothing

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: Four patients are on a medical unit. Which patient is at greatest risk for a fall within the next hour?

options.text: A patient who received a first dose of an opioid two hours ago and is standing at the bedside reaching into the closet
options.rationale: An opioid is a pain medication that also causes sedation and impairs balance. New impairment plus an unassisted high-risk movement is the combination that produces a fall.

options.text: A patient who has used a rolling walker at home for six years and is walking the hallway with it
options.rationale: Baseline function means what a patient could already do before this admission. This is the patient doing something right, offered as if it were evidence of risk.

options.text: A patient with a long-standing spinal cord injury who transfers from bed to wheelchair with a slide board and no help
options.rationale: A slide board is a transfer device that bridges two surfaces so the patient can shift across without standing. The severity of the diagnosis is not the same as instability.

options.text: A patient with a hemoglobin of 8.1 g/dL who is sitting in a chair with the call light clipped to the gown
options.rationale: Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells; a low value can cause weakness and dizziness on exertion. This is the most dramatic number in the question, which is exactly why it is offered.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk lives in the gap between what a patient can do and what the patient believes they can do. A limitation that is new and unrehearsed is more dangerous than one that is severe and familiar.

questions.stem: A patient is assessed at high risk for falls because of generalized weakness after eight days of illness. The patient can stand with the assistance of one person and walk ten feet before needing to rest. Which intervention does the nurse add to the plan of care?

options.text: Place the patient on bed rest and provide a bedside commode
options.rationale: Bed rest means restricting the patient to bed. The fall is postponed and made more likely, not prevented.

options.text: Assist the patient to walk a short distance three times daily and increase the distance as tolerated
options.rationale: Progressive ambulation means walking a set distance with help and extending it as strength returns. The patient already tolerates ten feet with one-person assistance, so a graded plan is safe and matched to current functional status.

options.text: Instruct the patient to remain in bed and to call before getting up
options.rationale: An instruction is information given to the patient; an intervention is something that changes the situation. Telling a weak patient not to move is a request, and it leaves the weakness untreated.

options.text: Request a bedside sitter to remind the patient to stay in bed
options.rationale: A sitter provides continuous observation, which is a genuine restraint alternative. Observation helps when it supports movement, not when it prevents it.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention is not immobility. Restriction produces the weakness that produces the next fall, so the plan should make movement safer rather than rarer.

questions.stem: A nurse enters a room and finds a patient sitting on the floor next to the bed. The patient is awake and says, 'I slipped getting up.' Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Help the patient back into bed
options.rationale: Moving a patient means changing position before the extent of injury is known. This is the right action in the wrong order.

options.text: Leave the room to get a lift and two more staff members
options.rationale: Leaving means the patient is unsupervised on the floor. The equipment will be needed, and going to fetch it abandons the patient at the moment they are least safe.

options.text: Call for assistance and stay with the patient
options.rationale: Calling for assistance means summoning help without leaving the room, by call light, alarm, or voice. Staying is what prevents a second event while help arrives.

options.text: Complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: An occurrence report is the internal safety report filed after an event. Documentation follows care, and choosing paperwork over a patient is the classic form of recording a problem in place of addressing it.

questions.takeaway: The post-fall sequence is call for assistance, stay with the patient, assess for injury, notify the provider, follow policy, reassess the plan, then document and file the occurrence report.

questions.stem: Which patient meets the criteria for restraint use?

options.text: A patient who wanders into other rooms at night on a unit staffed by two nurses
options.rationale: Staffing describes how many people are available to watch a patient. This option is sympathetic and true, which is what makes it tempting.

options.text: A patient with a high fall risk score whose family asks that a vest be used overnight
options.rationale: A fall risk score predicts the likelihood of falling. Honoring the request feels patient-centered and is not.

options.text: A patient who repeatedly refuses to stay in bed after hip surgery
options.rationale: Refusal means the patient is declining a request. Getting out of bed after hip surgery is a mobility and supervision problem, not a restraint indication, and restraining a competent patient for noncompliance is punishment.

options.text: A patient in delirium who has twice pulled at the endotracheal tube and continues reaching for it after reorientation, a sedation review, and a family member staying at the bedside
options.rationale: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating confusion with a physical cause. That combination is what the criteria require.

questions.takeaway: Two conditions must both be met: immediate harm the patient cannot safely control, and less restrictive options that were tried and were not enough.

questions.stem: A patient has bilateral soft wrist restraints in place. Which findings require the nurse to intervene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Range of motion has not been performed to either arm during this shift
options.rationale: Range of motion means moving a joint through its normal arc. Without it, joints stiffen and the patient loses function that was not lost to the illness.

options.text: The patient has voided 400 mL over the past four hours
options.rationale: Elimination is monitored during restraint use because a restrained patient cannot reach a bathroom. Four hundred milliliters over four hours is adequate output and evidence that the elimination need is being met.

options.text: The patient's spouse is sitting at the bedside reading aloud
options.rationale: Family presence is one of the listed restraint alternatives. It is something going right, offered in a list of things going wrong.

options.text: The patient is calm, fully oriented, and asks to have the restraints removed
options.rationale: The criterion for continuing a restraint is that the behavior threatening immediate harm is still present. A calm, oriented patient no longer meets criteria, and the standard is to remove at the earliest possible point rather than at a scheduled time.

options.text: Fingertips are cool and capillary refill is four seconds
options.rationale: Capillary refill is the time for color to return after pressing a nail bed, normally under three seconds. Cool fingertips plus delayed refill together point to compromised circulation distal to the restraint, which is one of the monitored areas and requires immediate release and reassessment.

options.text: The skin under the right wrist restraint is reddened and abraded
options.rationale: An abrasion is a scraped break in the skin surface. Broken skin under a restraint means friction is occurring, which will worsen with every movement until the device is removed or repadded.

questions.takeaway: While restraints are in use you monitor skin integrity, circulation, positioning, range of motion, hydration, elimination, and comfort and mental status. A finding in any of those areas is an action, not an observation.

questions.stem: A patient with dementia becomes agitated each evening. Which order, if carried out, would function as a chemical restraint?

options.text: Haloperidol given so the patient will settle and the night shift can manage the rest of the assignment
options.rationale: A chemical restraint is a medication given to control behavior rather than to treat a condition. Staff convenience is explicitly excluded as a reason to restrain.

options.text: Haloperidol given to treat hallucinations the patient describes as frightening
options.rationale: An antipsychotic given for psychotic symptoms is treating a condition the patient has. Only the purpose differs.

options.text: Acetaminophen given for a headache the patient reports at 1800
options.rationale: Acetaminophen is an analgesic. Treating pain is also one of the first things to rule out before restraining anyone.

options.text: Melatonin given at 2100 as part of the patient's usual home routine
options.rationale: Continuing a home medication maintains the patient's normal pattern. Preserving a familiar routine is closer to a restraint alternative than to a restraint.

questions.takeaway: What makes a medication a restraint is why it was given, not what it is. Ask whose problem the dose is solving.

questions.stem: A nurse raises all four side rails on the bed of a confused patient who keeps trying to get up. Which statement describes this action?

options.text: It is a universal fall precaution appropriate for every confused patient
options.rationale: Universal fall precautions are the baseline measures given to all patients, such as a low bed, locked brakes, and a reachable call light. Confusion calls for reorientation and familiar cues, not confinement.

options.text: It is a restraint, because the patient can no longer leave the bed freely
options.rationale: A restraint is any intervention that restricts free movement, including devices that are part of the bed. The effect on the patient is the same as a device strapped to the body, which is why full rails meet the definition and require the same justification and monitoring.

options.text: It is a safety measure that needs no order, because the rails are part of the bed
options.rationale: Ownership of the equipment does not change its effect. This is the belief that makes this the most commonly missed item in the topic.

options.text: It is appropriate as long as the patient's family agrees
options.rationale: Consent addresses whether care happens; criteria address whether it is indicated. Family preference does not convert an unjustified restraint into a justified one.

questions.takeaway: Restraint is defined by effect, not by hardware. Four rails up confines the patient, so it carries every restraint requirement.

questions.nursesNote: 0930: Admitted for community-acquired pneumonia. At home the patient walks to the bathroom without a device. Gets up twice each night to urinate. A diuretic was started this morning. Wears bifocals for reading only. On arrival the bed is in the high position from the transfer and the brakes are locked. The call light is coiled on the bedside table beyond the patient's reach. Personal belongings are in the closet across the room. The patient is wearing hospital socks with tread on both sides. Temperature 38.1 C, respirations 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. The patient asks that the overhead light be turned off and the room kept dark overnight.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that increase this patient's risk for a fall.

segments.text: At home the patient walks to the bathroom without a device
segments.rationale: Baseline function is what the patient could already do before admission. It is a strength offered among the risks.

segments.text: Gets up twice each night to urinate
segments.rationale: Nocturia means waking at night to urinate. Urgency and frequency are intrinsic fall risk factors precisely because they produce hurried trips in the dark.

segments.text: A diuretic was started this morning
segments.rationale: A diuretic increases urine production. It will increase the twice-nightly trips the patient already makes, and the patient has no experience of the new frequency.

segments.text: Wears bifocals for reading only
segments.rationale: Bifocals have separate distance and near zones and can distort the view of the floor when worn while walking. The detail is there to be checked, and it rules itself out.

segments.text: The bed is in the high position
segments.rationale: Bed height is an extrinsic fall risk factor. A patient sliding off a high bed lands before the feet are under the body, and correcting it takes seconds.

segments.text: The brakes are locked
segments.rationale: Locked brakes keep the bed from rolling during a transfer. It is something going right.

segments.text: The call light is coiled on the bedside table beyond the patient's reach
segments.rationale: A reachable call light is how a patient asks for help instead of getting up alone. An unreachable call light converts every need into an unassisted attempt.

segments.text: Personal belongings are in the closet across the room
segments.rationale: Keeping possessions within reach is a universal fall precaution. Very likely, and that trip is unplanned and unsupervised.

segments.text: Wearing hospital socks with tread on both sides
segments.rationale: Nonslip, well-fitting footwear is a universal precaution. This is appropriate footwear, not a hazard.

segments.text: Temperature 38.1 C, respirations 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air
segments.rationale: These are the vital signs expected with pneumonia. They are relevant to the illness and contribute nothing to the fall question.

segments.text: Asks that the overhead light be turned off and the room kept dark overnight
segments.rationale: Poor lighting is an extrinsic fall risk factor. A patient making extra unplanned trips in an unfamiliar dark room is the specific combination that produces night falls.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk is assembled from intrinsic factors that travel with the patient and extrinsic factors that belong to the room. The dangerous ones here only matter in combination: nocturia plus a new diuretic plus a dark room plus an unreachable call light.

questions.stem: Each patient has been assessed as being at risk for falls. For each patient, indicate the intervention that targets the identified risk factor.
columns: Improved lighting and access to eyeglasses
Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
Monitor symptoms and adjust medication timing

rows.text: Repeatedly starts for the bathroom the moment the urge is felt and has had two episodes of incontinence on the way
rows.rationale: Urgency means little warning between the urge and the need. Scheduled toileting does exactly that, which removes the hurried unassisted trip rather than forbidding it.

rows.text: Reaches for the arm of the chair, misses it by several inches, and has walked into the bedside table twice
rows.answer: Improved lighting and access to eyeglasses
rows.rationale: Misjudging distance is a spatial perception problem. Repeated contact with objects that are where they belong points to vision, and lighting and glasses are the targeted fix.

rows.text: Asks what building this is each time someone enters and has twice tried to leave to 'get to work'
rows.rationale: Disorientation means the patient has the wrong model of where and when they are. Reorientation and familiar cues correct the belief, which removes the reason for the attempt.

rows.text: Can stand unaided but must stop and hold the handrail after about six feet
rows.answer: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
rows.rationale: Reduced endurance and strength impair balance as the patient tires. Assisted transfers and ambulation do both, which is why the goal is safe movement rather than rest.

rows.text: Became unsteady on standing within two hours of the first dose of a new antihypertensive given this morning
rows.answer: Monitor symptoms and adjust medication timing
rows.rationale: An antihypertensive lowers blood pressure and can cause unsteadiness on standing. Monitoring symptoms and adjusting when the dose is given addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

rows.text: Has been on bed rest for five days and now needs two people to move from lying to sitting
rows.answer: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
rows.rationale: Deconditioning is loss of strength from disuse. This is the second row in the set with the same intervention, because two different histories produced the same risk factor.

answer.r2: Improved lighting and access to eyeglasses
answer.r4: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
answer.r5: Monitor symptoms and adjust medication timing
answer.r6: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation

questions.takeaway: Every patient at risk for falls gets the universal precautions. The individualized plan is built by naming which risk factor is driving this patient's risk and choosing the intervention that targets it.

questions.scenario: At 0200 on the third day after abdominal surgery, a patient becomes restless, repeatedly pulls at the nasogastric tube, and tries to swing both legs over the side rail. The last dose of analgesia was given eight hours ago. The patient grimaces when the abdomen is touched and answers questions in single words. Heart rate is 104, blood pressure 148 over 88, temperature 37.1 C, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. The abdomen is soft with bowel sounds present and the nasogastric tube is draining as expected.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Restraint is permitted only for immediate harm the patient cannot control, after alternatives have failed. This is the right category of concern acted on before the assessment that should precede it.

options.text: Stay with the patient and secure the nasogastric tube while the analgesic takes effect
options.rationale: Continuous observation is a restraint alternative that protects the device without restricting the patient. Yes, and it requires no order and causes no harm.

options.text: Document that the patient is confused and pulling at the tube
options.rationale: Documentation records what was found. It also mislabels the finding, because the stem describes pain behavior rather than confusion.

options.text: Assess the pain and administer the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Assessment before intervention means establishing what the problem is before treating it. Eight hours without analgesia, grimacing on palpation, and a heart rate and blood pressure elevated by sympathetic response all name unrelieved pain.

options.text: Unrelieved postoperative pain
options.rationale: Unrelieved pain is pain that has outlasted the last dose of analgesia. The pieces fit together only under this heading.

options.text: Nasogastric tube malfunction
options.rationale: Malfunction means the device is not working as intended. The finding is there to be checked and it excludes this option.

options.text: Delirium from an undetermined cause
options.rationale: Delirium is acute fluctuating confusion with a physical cause. This is the near-miss, because agitation at night after surgery is often delirium and a patient in pain can look confused.

options.text: Nonadherence to the postoperative plan
options.rationale: Nonadherence means declining to follow agreed treatment. Labeling a patient in pain as nonadherent replaces a mechanism with a judgment.

options.text: Whether the patient stops reaching for the nasogastric tube
options.rationale: The behavior was the presenting problem. Behavior returning to baseline is the evidence that the hypothesis was right.

options.text: Nasogastric output volume over the next shift
options.rationale: Output volume measures how much the tube is draining. The tube was already draining as expected, so this measures something that was never the problem.

options.text: Reported pain rating one hour after the analgesic is given
options.rationale: A pain rating is the patient's own score for pain intensity. It is also the measure that does not depend on the nurse's interpretation of behavior.

options.text: Whether a family member is able to stay overnight
options.rationale: Family presence is a useful alternative for confusion and fear. It is a resource, not an outcome.

questions.takeaway: Agitation is a symptom, so you look for its cause before you restrict the patient. Pain, toileting needs, hunger, thirst, delirium, medication effects, fear, overstimulation, and an unfamiliar environment are the list to work through.

questions.stem: A nurse is admitting a patient who uses a cane at home. Which question best identifies what is new about this patient's mobility?

options.text: Do you feel safe walking at home?
options.rationale: Asks about perception, not about change. Useful, but it does not compare before with now.

options.text: How long have you used the cane?
options.rationale: Establishes duration of a long-standing device. Long use means practiced skill, not new risk.

options.text: What could you do a month ago that you cannot do today?
options.rationale: Directly compares baseline with current ability. New deficits are the ones the patient has not yet adapted to.

options.text: Has your doctor told you that you are a fall risk?
options.rationale: Asks what someone else concluded. It does not assess this patient's current function.

questions.takeaway: Separate baseline from new. The new deficit is the dangerous one.

questions.stem: A nurse finds an unlabeled syringe left on a medication cart. No patient was harmed. Which action best supports a culture of safety?

options.text: Discard the syringe and continue the medication pass
options.rationale: Removes the hazard today and leaves the process that created it unchanged.

options.text: Ask coworkers who left it so they can be corrected
options.rationale: Focuses on the person. Blame suppresses future reporting, which is what a culture of safety depends on.

options.text: Mention it in the end-of-shift handoff
options.rationale: Passes information to a few people. It never reaches anyone who can change the process.

options.text: Report it so the labeling process can be reviewed
options.rationale: A near miss is free information about a hazard. Reporting sends it to people who can change the system.

questions.takeaway: Near misses are the cheapest safety data a unit gets. Report the hazard, not the person.

questions.stem: A unit has had four missed hourly rounding checks this month. Which change best reduces reliance on memory?

options.text: Add an automated prompt at each rounding interval
options.rationale: Puts the reminder in the workflow at the moment of action instead of in a person's head.

options.text: Post a reminder sign in the break room
options.rationale: Depends on someone reading it and then remembering hours later.

options.text: Ask nurses to set alarms on their personal phones
options.rationale: An individual workaround. It fails silently and nobody can see whose alarm was never set.

options.text: Discuss the misses at annual performance reviews
options.rationale: Addresses the individual after the fact and changes none of the conditions that produced the miss.

questions.takeaway: Design the system for a tired nurse, not an ideal one.

questions.stem: During a post-fall huddle the team finds the patient was wearing smooth-soled slippers brought from home and the floor had been recently mopped. Which conclusion does this support?

options.text: The patient was noncompliant with the safety plan
options.rationale: A label rather than a mechanism. Wearing one's own slippers is not refusal of care.

options.text: Extrinsic factors contributed and the environment needs to change
options.rationale: Footwear and wet floors belong to the room and the routine. Both are correctable for every patient.

options.text: The fall risk score was inaccurate
options.rationale: The score describes the patient. Nothing here suggests the patient's own risks were misjudged.

options.text: The fall could not have been prevented
options.rationale: Nonslip footwear and a dry floor are universal precautions. Both were available and neither was in place.

questions.takeaway: The huddle asks what contributed and what changes, not who was careless.

questions.stem: Which actions are part of universal fall precautions applied to every patient? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep floor surfaces clean and dry
options.rationale: Spills are an extrinsic hazard corrected for all patients, not a patient-specific intervention.

options.text: Have the patient demonstrate use of the call light
options.rationale: Demonstration verifies the patient can actually work it. Telling them where it is proves nothing.

options.text: Keep personal possessions within reach
options.rationale: Removes the unplanned trip across the room to retrieve something.

options.text: Keep the bed in the low position with brakes locked
options.rationale: Reduces fall height and prevents the bed rolling during transfer. Applied to everyone.

options.text: Order a bedside sitter for every patient over 65
options.rationale: Age alone does not trigger one-to-one observation, and sitters are not a universal measure.

options.text: Apply a vest restraint at night
options.rationale: Restraints are never used for routine fall prevention.

questions.takeaway: Universal precautions need no assessment. They fix the room and the routine.

questions.stem: A confused patient keeps trying to climb out of bed. Which action does the nurse take before considering restraints?

options.text: Raise all four side rails
options.rationale: Full rails restrict free movement, so this is itself a restraint.

options.text: Obtain a restraint order so it is ready if needed
options.rationale: An available order is not an indication, and it skips the assessment that should come first.

options.text: Assess for pain, a full bladder, hunger, or thirst
options.rationale: Behavior is communication. Most nighttime agitation has a fixable cause, and restraint leaves that cause in place.

options.text: Move the patient to a room farther from the nurses' station
options.rationale: Reduces observation of a patient who is actively unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Ask why before you restrict. Pain, toileting, hunger, thirst, delirium, medication, fear, overstimulation.

questions.stem: A patient in soft wrist restraints has been calm and oriented for the past two hours and is asking to have them removed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep them on until the provider rounds in the morning
options.rationale: Removal is based on the patient's behavior, not on a schedule or a rounding time.

options.text: Loosen one restraint and leave the other in place
options.rationale: A partial restraint is still a restraint and still requires an indication that no longer exists.

options.text: Explain that the restraints must stay on for the full ordered time
options.rationale: An order sets a maximum, not a minimum. Restraints are removed as early as possible.

options.text: Remove the restraints and continue to monitor
options.rationale: The criterion for continuing is that the dangerous behavior is still present. It is not, so the restraint comes off at the earliest point.

questions.takeaway: Reassess the need continuously and remove at the earliest point.

questions.stem: Four patients were admitted last night. All four were independent at home. Which patient is most likely to be injured by the hospitalization itself rather than by the illness?

options.text: A patient with a urinary tract infection started on a sedating antihistamine for sleep, with the bathroom on the far side of the room
options.rationale: Hospitalization raises risk through changed routine, new medications, sleep disruption, and unfamiliar surroundings. This patient has a new sedating drug plus an unfamiliar path to the toilet at night, and neither existed at home.

options.text: A patient with pneumonia and an oxygen saturation of 91 percent on room air
options.rationale: Acute illness is its own risk, and the finding describes disease severity rather than something the hospital introduced.

options.text: A patient admitted for observation after a syncopal episode, now on continuous telemetry
options.rationale: Monitoring is a tether and this patient is also being watched closely. Syncope is the illness, not a hospital-created hazard.

options.text: A patient with cellulitis receiving intravenous antibiotics every eight hours
options.rationale: A line is a tether, and intermittent antibiotics in an otherwise well patient add little beyond the illness itself.

questions.takeaway: Ask what the building added. New medication plus unfamiliar layout plus disrupted sleep is the combination that injures a previously independent patient.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught the family of a patient at high risk for falls. Which statement by a family member indicates that the teaching needs to be reinforced?

options.text: I will put the water and the glasses on the table by the bed before I leave
options.rationale: Keeping possessions within reach removes the unplanned trip across the room. Correct understanding.

options.text: If nobody answers the call light right away, I will help walk to the bathroom myself
options.rationale: The plan specifies who assists and how. A family member substituting for trained assistance is the well-intentioned version of an unassisted transfer, and it is the statement that needs correction.

options.text: I will tell the nurse if the confusion seems worse in the evening
options.rationale: Reporting concerning behavior is exactly what families are asked to do.

options.text: I brought the shoes with the rubber soles instead of the slippers
options.rationale: Nonslip, well-fitting footwear is a universal precaution, and footwear is the thing families can fix in a day.

questions.takeaway: Family education specifies the assistance needed. Willingness to help is not the same as being the assistance the plan calls for.

questions.stem: A nurse is supervising assistive personnel caring for four patients on a fall prevention protocol. Which observed action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Assistive personnel lower a bed and confirm the brakes are locked after a bath
options.rationale: Maintaining a safe environment is delegable and this is the task carried out correctly.

options.text: Assistive personnel take a patient to the bathroom at the scheduled time and stay in the room
options.rationale: Assisting with toileting on a set schedule is delegable and the assistance level was already determined.

options.text: Assistive personnel tell a patient who is asking to walk that the patient seems steady enough to go alone today
options.rationale: Judging whether a patient may ambulate unassisted is an assessment. Assistive personnel may assist with mobility according to the plan; they may not decide what the plan should be.

options.text: Assistive personnel report that a patient has been picking at the intravenous dressing
options.rationale: Reporting concerning behavior is delegable. Observation travels; interpretation does not.

questions.takeaway: Delegation moves the doing. The moment an option has assistive personnel judging readiness, it is wrong.

questions.stem: A patient who is confused becomes increasingly restless at 2100 and repeatedly tries to get out of bed. Which nursing actions are appropriate before restraint is considered? Select all that apply.

options.text: Offer toileting and assess for bladder distention
options.rationale: Toileting need is one of the first causes to assess. A full bladder is a common and fixable driver of nighttime restlessness.

options.text: Ask a family member to stay at the bedside
options.rationale: Family presence is a listed alternative and works directly on confusion and fear.

options.text: Dim the overhead lighting and turn off the television
options.rationale: Environmental modification addresses excess stimulation, which is a named cause of the behavior.

options.text: Administer the ordered antipsychotic to settle the patient for the night
options.rationale: A medication given to control behavior rather than to treat a condition is a chemical restraint, not an alternative to one.

options.text: Activate a bed exit alarm and reposition the patient closer to the nurses' station
options.rationale: Alarms and observation are listed alternatives. They notify without restricting movement.

options.text: Tuck the sheets tightly across the chest to discourage rising
options.rationale: Anything that restricts free movement is a restraint by definition, regardless of what it is made of.

questions.takeaway: Assess the cause, then reorient, involve family, modify the environment, meet the need, and use alarms.

questions.stem: A patient has been in a vest restraint for six hours for pulling at a chest tube. At 0300 the nurse finds the patient partly over the side rail with the vest twisted across the upper chest, breathing rapidly, and unable to speak in full sentences. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Call for assistance and stay with the patient
options.rationale: Help is needed and will be summoned, and the compression continues while it arrives. This is the right instinct in the wrong order.

options.text: Assess circulation and skin integrity under the restraint
options.rationale: Both are monitored during restraint use. Neither addresses a patient who cannot complete a sentence.

options.text: Notify the provider that the restraint is no longer effective
options.rationale: Escalation follows the intervention. Reporting first leaves the chest compressed while the call is placed.

options.text: Release the restraint and reposition the patient
options.rationale: A twisted vest across the chest of a patient who has climbed partway out is an active airway and breathing threat. Releasing it removes the compression, and it is the one thing that cannot wait.

questions.takeaway: The most serious restraint injuries happen to patients trying to escape one. Airway and breathing outrank every monitoring parameter.

questions.stem: A unit's fall rate has not changed in six months despite an updated fall protocol. Reviewing the data, the manager finds that most falls were unwitnessed, occurred between 0200 and 0500, and involved patients whose documented plans included scheduled toileting. Which conclusion does this best support?

options.text: The scheduled toileting is not reaching the patients overnight
options.rationale: Documented plans that fail at one specific time of day point to execution rather than design. The plan exists on paper and the overnight round is not happening.

options.text: The protocol itself is clinically incorrect and needs rewriting
options.rationale: The plans named an appropriate intervention. Nothing in the pattern suggests the wrong intervention was chosen.

options.text: These patients were assessed at too low a risk level
options.rationale: They were assessed as needing scheduled toileting, so the assessment identified the risk correctly.

options.text: Falls at night are unavoidable on a unit with reduced overnight staffing
options.rationale: Staffing as an explanation ends the inquiry. A time-specific pattern is a process finding, not an inevitability.

questions.takeaway: Falls cost injury, confidence, length of stay, and reimbursement. Ask whether the plan reached the bedside before asking whether the plan was right.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a stroke has expressive aphasia and new right-sided weakness. The patient understands what is said but cannot produce words reliably, and has twice been found sitting at the edge of the bed alone. Which addition to the fall prevention plan is most important?

options.text: Place the call light on the unaffected side and establish a signal the patient can use without speaking
options.rationale: Communication impairment means the usual way of summoning help has failed, and weakness means the patient cannot compensate physically. Restoring a usable way to call is what stops the unassisted attempts.

options.text: Ask the patient to verbally confirm understanding of the safety instructions each shift
options.rationale: Expressive aphasia is exactly the inability to produce reliable speech. Requiring a verbal response tests the deficit rather than working around it.

options.text: Post a fall risk sign above the bed and document the risk level each shift
options.rationale: Signage and documentation record the risk. Neither gives the patient a way to ask for help at the moment of getting up.

options.text: Raise all four side rails while the patient is in bed
options.rationale: Full rails restrict free movement, which makes them a restraint, and restraints are never used for routine fall prevention.

questions.takeaway: Sensory, cognitive, and communication impairments raise risk because the patient cannot call for help. Restore the signal before adding anything else.

questions.stem: A patient who was oriented on admission is pulling at an IV line at 0200 and does not recognize the room. Assistive personnel are asking for wrist restraints. Which actions help the nurse decide whether a restraint is needed? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chart the agitated behavior and the number of times the line was touched
options.rationale: Documentation records what happened. It is required, but it produces no information about why the behavior is occurring and does not move the decision forward.

options.text: Palpate the bladder and check the time of last voiding
options.rationale: Urinary retention means urine collecting in a bladder that is not emptying. A full bladder is one of the most common and most reversible causes of sudden agitation in an older patient.

options.text: Ask the family to sign consent for the restraint
options.rationale: Consent addresses permission, not need. Obtaining it before assessing the cause skips the step that determines whether a restraint is justified at all.

options.text: Review the medications given in the past 12 hours
options.rationale: Many drugs given at night, including opioids and sedatives, cause confusion in older adults. A new drug is a treatable cause, and treating it may remove the reason for the restraint.

options.text: Measure oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Hypoxia means not enough oxygen reaching the tissues, and the brain shows it first as restlessness and confusion. It is fast to check and dangerous to miss.

options.text: Check the most recent serum sodium and glucose
options.rationale: Sodium and glucose imbalances both alter mental status. These values identify a metabolic cause that can be corrected instead of restrained.

questions.takeaway: Agitation is a symptom with a cause. Before a restraint is considered, the assessment is aimed at finding a cause you can treat: retention, medications, oxygenation, and metabolic values.

questions.stem: A patient with liver failure has a prothrombin time of 28 seconds, with a reference range of 11 to 13 seconds. The patient is scored at high risk for falls, is alert and oriented, and consistently uses the call light before getting up. Which intervention is targeted to this patient's greatest risk?

options.text: Place a bed exit alarm
options.rationale: A bed alarm signals that a patient is getting up unassisted. This patient already calls before getting up, so the alarm addresses a behavior that is not occurring.

options.text: Keep the call light within the patient's reach
options.rationale: Keeping the call light in reach is a universal fall precaution applied to every patient. It is correct care, but it is not targeted to anything specific about this patient.

options.text: Provide a protective helmet when the patient is up in a chair or walking
options.rationale: A prolonged prothrombin time means blood takes much longer than normal to clot. This patient may not fall more often than others, but a head strike could cause bleeding inside the skull, so the intervention targets the severity of injury rather than the chance of falling.

options.text: Schedule oral medications at least two hours before bedtime
options.rationale: Adjusting medication timing reduces nighttime urgency and sedation. Nothing in this patient's information points to either problem.

questions.takeaway: When a patient has a bleeding disorder, fall prevention shifts from preventing the fall to preventing the injury. Match the intervention to what is actually most dangerous for that patient.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to help a patient back to bed one day after knee replacement. The patient is sitting in a bedside chair. Which findings require the nurse to act before starting the transfer? Select all that apply.

options.text: The bed is in the high position
options.rationale: A bed above the patient's seated height forces them to climb rather than pivot, and increases the distance of any fall. The bed is lowered before the transfer.

options.text: The IV pump has a current safety inspection sticker
options.rationale: A current inspection sticker is how you know equipment has been checked and is safe to use. This is a normal finding, not a hazard.

options.text: The bed brakes are unlocked
options.rationale: Unlocked brakes let the bed roll away as the patient bears weight on it. Locking them is done before the patient moves, not during.

options.text: A walker is positioned within reach of the chair
options.rationale: Having the prescribed assistive device nearby supports a safe transfer after knee surgery. This is something set up correctly.

options.text: No gait belt is available in the room
options.rationale: A gait belt is a belt around the waist that gives the nurse a safe place to hold. Without it, staff tend to pull on the arm or under the armpit, which injures the shoulder.

options.text: The patient's glasses are on a table across the room
options.rationale: Vision contributes to balance and to judging distance. Transferring a patient who cannot see the bed clearly adds a risk that is removed by handing over the glasses.

questions.takeaway: Before any transfer, set the environment first: bed low and locked, device and gait belt at hand, and the patient able to see. Two of the findings in a list like this are usually things already done right.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses four patients at the start of the shift. Which patient is most likely to become violent toward staff?

options.text: Moves restlessly in bed, swears and grimaces when coughing, and speaks quietly
options.rationale: Swearing during a painful movement is an expression of pain, not aggression. The quiet voice and the link to coughing point to discomfort that needs treating.

options.text: Is very drowsy, loses attention during questions, and mumbles when speaking
options.rationale: Drowsiness and poor attention suggest sedation or delirium. This patient is at risk for falls and aspiration, but is not showing behavior directed at staff.

options.text: Maintains eye contact, is calm during the assessment, and asks frequent questions
options.rationale: Asking many questions shows engagement with care. Calm participation is the opposite of the pattern that predicts violence.

options.text: Speaks in a loud voice, becomes irritable when approached to walk, and is disoriented to place
options.rationale: Altered mental status is the most common feature of people who become violent in health care settings, and rising voice with irritability on approach is escalating behavior. The two together are the warning.

questions.takeaway: Violence risk is predicted by altered mental status plus escalating behavior. Pain, sedation, and anxiety produce difficult behavior that is not aggression, and treating them is the intervention.

questions.stem: At 0400 a patient is found walking in the hallway, confused, saying, "I can't find the bathroom." The patient last voided at 2200. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Request an order for a wrist restraint
options.rationale: A restraint is used only when there is immediate danger and less restrictive measures have failed. Walking to find the bathroom is a met need, not a danger.

options.text: Assist the patient to the bathroom now
options.rationale: The patient has stated the need and has not voided in six hours. Meeting the need is both the immediate intervention and the reason the patient got up.

options.text: Request an order for an indwelling urinary catheter
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter drains the bladder through a tube. It is invasive, raises infection risk, and is not a solution for a patient who can walk to the bathroom with help.

options.text: Begin scheduled toileting every 2 to 3 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting offers the bathroom before the urge becomes urgent. It removes the reason for unassisted walking rather than reacting after it happens.

options.text: Raise all four side rails and place the bed in the high position
options.rationale: Four rails raised to keep a patient in bed is a restraint, and a high bed increases the distance of a fall. This combination causes the injury it is meant to prevent.

options.text: Keep the path from the bed to the bathroom clear and lit
options.rationale: Clutter and darkness are environmental fall risks. Fixing them supports safe movement instead of preventing movement.

questions.takeaway: A confused patient who gets up is usually trying to meet a need. Meet the need, then change the schedule and the environment so the patient does not have to get up alone next time.

questions.stem: A patient sitting in a bedside chair suddenly cries out, stiffens, and begins jerking. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Insert an oral airway to protect the tongue
options.rationale: Nothing is placed in the mouth once a seizure has started. It breaks teeth, can obstruct the airway, and injures whoever attempts it.

options.text: Ease the patient to the floor and protect the head
options.rationale: A seizure in a chair carries the risk of falling and striking the head. Lowering the patient to the floor and cushioning the head prevents the injury the seizure would otherwise cause.

options.text: Hold the arms and legs still to stop the jerking
options.rationale: Holding a convulsing patient down causes fractures and soft tissue injury. Limbs are guided away from hard objects, not restrained.

options.text: Lift the patient into the bed
options.rationale: A patient is not moved from the floor to the bed while a seizure is in progress. Lifting a jerking patient risks injury to the patient and to the nurse.

questions.takeaway: During a seizure you protect and position, you do not restrain and you do not put anything in the mouth. Note the time, stay with the patient, and turn them on their side once the movements stop.

questions.stem: A nurse sees flames in the bathroom of a patient's room. The patient is in bed and cannot walk without assistance. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Close the bathroom door to contain the fire
options.rationale: Confining the fire limits its spread and is the third step. Closing a door does not help the patient who is still in the room.

options.text: Activate the fire alarm and report the exact location
options.rationale: Activating the alarm brings help and is the second step. It is correct, and it is not first while a patient who cannot move is still beside the fire.

options.text: Move the patient out of the room
options.rationale: Rescue comes first. A patient near a fire is in immediate danger and cannot move without help, so removing them precedes every other step.

options.text: Get the extinguisher, pull the pin, and aim at the base of the flames
options.rationale: Extinguishing is the last step, and only for a small contained fire. Fighting a fire before moving an endangered patient reverses the priority.

questions.takeaway: RACE sets the order: rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish. The step people reach for first is the extinguisher, and it is the last one.

questions.stem: A patient is found on the floor beside the bed. No one saw what happened. The patient is alert and oriented, reports no pain, and has no visible injury. Which entry is appropriate for the medical record?

options.text: "Patient found on floor beside bed. Alert and oriented. No visible injury. Provider notified."
options.rationale: Documentation records what was observed and what was done. Because no one saw the event, found on the floor is the only accurate description of it.

options.text: "Patient fell while attempting to get up without assistance. Occurrence report completed."
options.rationale: An occurrence report is a confidential internal document for quality review. Naming it in the chart pulls it into the legal record, and the cause described was not witnessed.

options.text: "Patient fell because the call light was out of reach."
options.rationale: This states a cause that no one observed. Charting a conclusion rather than a finding records an assumption as fact.

options.text: "Patient slipped getting out of bed. Assistive personnel did not answer the call light in time."
options.rationale: This assigns blame to a staff member and describes an unwitnessed sequence. The medical record documents the patient, not an investigation of staff.

questions.takeaway: Chart what you saw and what you did. For an unwitnessed fall that means found on the floor, never a cause, never blame, and never a reference to the occurrence report.

questions.stem: About 50 mL of a chemotherapy drug spills onto the floor beside a patient's bed. The patient is in bed and is not in contact with the spill, and no staff member has touched it. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Open the window to ventilate the room
options.rationale: Ventilation helps with gases and vapors. A liquid spill on the floor is a contact hazard, so airing the room does not reduce the risk.

options.text: Consult the drug's safety data sheet before beginning cleanup
options.rationale: A safety data sheet lists a chemical's hazards, the protective equipment required, first aid, and the steps for containment and removal. Handling a hazardous drug without that information risks exposure through the skin.

options.text: Wipe up the spill with the bed linens and place them in the regular trash
options.rationale: This puts bare hands near a hazardous drug and sends contaminated material into general waste. Both steps spread the exposure rather than containing it.

options.text: Document the volume spilled and notify pharmacy for a replacement dose
options.rationale: Replacing the dose matters, and documentation is required. Neither addresses a hazardous substance sitting on the floor right now.

questions.takeaway: Chemical exposure starts with the safety data sheet, because it tells you the protective equipment and cleanup method before you touch anything. Know where they are kept on your unit before you need one.

questions.stem: A patient is placed in bilateral wrist restraints at 1400 for violent behavior after striking a staff member. Which actions meet the standard of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Obtain a provider order stating the type, location, reason, and duration of the restraint
options.rationale: A restraint must be clinically justified and part of the prescribed plan of care. An order that does not state what, where, why, and how long does not meet the requirement.

options.text: Ensure a provider assesses the patient face to face within 60 minutes
options.rationale: Restraint for violent or self-destructive behavior requires a face-to-face provider assessment within one hour. This is the check on whether the restraint was justified.

options.text: Obtain a PRN order so the restraint can be reapplied if the behavior returns
options.rationale: PRN means as needed. Restraints may never be ordered this way, because each episode requires its own decision and its own order.

options.text: Monitor the patient continuously
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring is required for a patient restrained for violent behavior, in person or by video. Every two hours applies to nonviolent restraint, not to this patient.

options.text: Secure the restraint ties to the side rails so they can be reached quickly
options.rationale: Ties are secured to the bed frame. A restraint tied to a rail tightens on the limb when the rail is lowered, which can injure the arm.

options.text: Plan for the order to be renewed after no more than 4 hours
options.rationale: Each order and renewal is limited to 4 hours for an adult, 2 hours for ages 9 through 17, and 1 hour under age 9. The limit forces a fresh decision about whether the restraint is still needed.

questions.takeaway: Restraint for violent behavior carries the strictest rules: a specific order, a provider assessment within 60 minutes, continuous monitoring, and renewal at 4 hours for an adult. Never PRN, and never tied to a side rail.

questions.stem: A patient who managed independently at home has been kept in bed for six days during treatment for an infection. The patient now needs two people to move from lying to sitting. Which statement best explains this change?

options.text: Prolonged rest reduced muscle strength, and the patient is now unable to move safely without help
options.rationale: Deconditioning is the loss of strength and endurance that follows disuse. Muscle weakens quickly without load, which is why restriction is not a neutral choice and why immobility is itself a fall risk factor.

options.text: The infection has extended and is producing new neurologic weakness
options.rationale: Neurologic weakness comes from damage to nerves or the brain and usually appears in a pattern, such as one side or one limb group. A spreading infection is a real possibility to rule out, and nothing here points to it.

options.text: The patient has become unmotivated to participate in care
options.rationale: Motivation describes willingness. Substituting a judgment about the patient for a mechanism is how real causes get missed.

options.text: This degree of change is an expected part of aging and will resolve once the patient is home
options.rationale: Expected aging changes develop gradually over years. Attributing an acute functional loss to age leaves a reversible problem untreated.

questions.takeaway: Immobility produces the weakness that produces falls. A functional loss that appears over days has a cause you can name and usually reverse.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel tells the nurse that a patient 'looks strong enough to walk to the door alone today.' Which response does the nurse make?

options.text: If the patient seems steady once you are up, it is fine to let go partway
options.rationale: Letting go mid-ambulation is a change in the level of assistance. Judging readiness is nursing judgment and does not transfer with the task.

options.text: Walk with the patient at the assistance level on the plan, and tell me what you notice
options.rationale: Delegation transfers a task while the nurse keeps the decision and the outcome. The task proceeds at the specified level, and the observation returns to the nurse, who is the one who may change the plan.

options.text: Leave the patient in bed until I am able to get there myself
options.rationale: Deferring the activity means the patient does not move today. This sounds cautious and quietly chooses immobility.

options.text: Document that the patient walked independently today
options.rationale: Documentation records what happened. Recording an outcome that was never observed is both inaccurate and unsafe for whoever reads it next.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel may assist with mobility according to the plan. Deciding what the plan should be, and deciding mid-task to change it, stays with the nurse.

questions.stem: A patient was kept in restraints in bed for two days because of severe agitation during an acute illness. The restraints were removed this morning. Which finding indicates a complication of the restraints rather than a feature of the illness?

options.text: The temperature is 38.0 C
options.rationale: Fever is a systemic response to infection or inflammation. This belongs to whatever brought the patient in.

options.text: The white blood cell count remains elevated
options.rationale: White blood cells rise in response to infection and inflammation. It tracks the underlying illness.

options.text: The patient cannot bear weight to stand and needs two people to pivot to the chair
options.rationale: Loss of mobility is one of the listed complications of restraint. Muscle strength falls quickly without load, and this is the deficit that was created by the treatment rather than by the disease.

options.text: The patient reports a dry mouth after taking nothing by mouth overnight
options.rationale: Dry mouth follows reduced oral intake. Hydration is a genuine monitoring area during restraint use, and this particular finding is already explained.

questions.takeaway: Restraints cause skin and neurovascular injury, increased agitation and confusion, loss of mobility, and injury sustained trying to escape. Two days held still is enough to cost a patient the strength to stand.

questions.stem: A patient's fall prevention plan lists weakness as the primary risk factor. Which addition to the plan most directly addresses that risk factor?

options.text: A bed alarm set to sound when the patient sits up
options.rationale: A bed alarm signals that movement has already started. It is detection offered in place of prevention.

options.text: Moving the patient to a room closer to the nurses' station
options.rationale: Proximity shortens response time. It is a reasonable supporting measure and it treats nothing.

options.text: Scheduled toileting every one to two hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting prevents hurried trips driven by urgency. This is a correct intervention aimed at a different problem, which is the most common way a fall prevention question goes wrong.

options.text: A referral for a strengthening and gait program with progressive ambulation
options.rationale: A strengthening and gait program builds muscle and retrains walking under supervision. Weakness is treated by graded use, and the therapist, nurse, and assistive personnel share the work of carrying it out.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the named risk factor. Interventions that detect movement or shorten response time are useful, and they do not treat the deficit.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient who has been on bed rest for five days is getting up for the first time. Before standing, the nurse has the patient sit at the edge of the bed. The patient says the room is 'swimming,' and the heart rate rises from 78 to 106.

The finding that most increases the risk for injury at this moment is [[1]].

The nurse's next action is to [[2]].

The change that would show the plan is working is [[3]].

options.text: the patient's report of boredom during the stay
options.rationale: Boredom describes how the stay has felt. It is true and inert.

options.text: the five days of bed rest
options.rationale: Bed rest is the exposure that produced the deconditioning. This is the genuine near miss in the pair.

options.text: a two-pound weight loss since admission
options.rationale: A small weight change over a short admission is common and nonspecific. No, and it is the kind of measured value that looks meaningful because it has a number attached.

options.text: the dizziness and the rise in heart rate on sitting up
options.rationale: Together these describe the body failing to keep blood pressure stable when the patient changes position. Read as a pair they mean the patient is not ready to stand.

options.text: ask assistive personnel to walk the patient while you finish charting
options.rationale: Handing off an activity means transferring it at the assistance level on the plan. Delegating an activity the patient is not currently tolerating passes the risk to someone with less authority to stop it.

options.text: assist the patient to stand immediately so the episode passes
options.rationale: Standing raises the head further above the heart. This is the moment the patient is most likely to fall.

options.text: keep the patient sitting and supported until the symptoms settle, then recheck before standing
options.rationale: Sitting at the edge of the bed lets the circulation adjust to the upright position in stages. It treats the symptom, preserves the mobility plan, and creates a checkpoint before the riskiest part.

options.text: help the patient lie back down and cancel the activity for the day
options.rationale: Canceling returns the patient to bed. The symptom needs managing, not the activity abandoning.

options.text: the patient agrees to get up again tomorrow
options.rationale: Agreement is a statement of intent. A patient can be entirely willing and still become dizzy on sitting.

options.text: the patient sits and then stands without dizziness and walks the planned distance with the planned assistance
options.rationale: An outcome is a change in the patient, stated in terms of what the patient can do. It names position change without symptoms, and distance with a specified assistance level, both of which can be observed and compared.

options.text: the bed alarm does not sound during the shift
options.rationale: A silent alarm means no unassisted movement was detected. Only that the patient stayed put, which is the opposite of the goal.

options.text: the family reports the patient seems more cheerful
options.rationale: Mood is worth knowing and is reported by someone else. Ask: does it measure whether the patient can change position and walk safely? No.

questions.takeaway: After a period of restricted movement, getting up is staged. Symptoms on sitting are the checkpoint, and the outcome is stated as what the patient can do, not as what the patient intends or how the patient feels.

questions.stem: A nurse tests the strength of a patient's right leg. The patient can slide the leg sideways across the mattress but cannot lift it off the bed. Which grade does the nurse document?

options.text: Grade 2
options.rationale: Grade 2 is movement without gravity, meaning the limb moves when the pull of gravity is taken out of the plane of motion. It cannot lift against gravity, so it sits one grade below that.

options.text: Grade 1
options.rationale: Grade 1 is a trace contraction, meaning the muscle flickers under the skin without producing movement at the joint. Movement rules this grade out.

options.text: Grade 3
options.rationale: Grade 3 is movement against gravity, meaning the limb can be raised off the surface but holds nothing added. No, and that is exactly the boundary between grade 2 and grade 3.

options.text: Grade 4
options.rationale: Grade 4 is movement against some resistance, meaning the patient lifts the limb and holds it while you press against it. You cannot reach grade 4 without first clearing gravity.

questions.takeaway: Grade 3 is the hinge in the strength scale: it is the grade where the limb just clears gravity. Below 3 the movement only happens in a supported plane, and above 3 you are adding resistance.

questions.stem: A nurse has just repositioned a patient from supine to a side-lying position. The patient has a nasogastric tube, a urinary catheter, and an intravenous line. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document the time of the position change and the position used
options.rationale: Documentation records what was done. Charting follows the reassessment rather than replacing it, and a problem created by the turn would go unfound.

options.text: Reassess alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and the ability to breathe comfortably
options.rationale: Reassessment after repositioning checks what the move itself changed. With three devices in place, a tube caught under the patient or pulled taut is the predictable harm, and it is found in the minute after the turn or not at all.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees to support breathing
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed supports lung expansion and is part of supported Fowler's positioning. Changing the position again undoes the turn before anyone has checked it.

options.text: Return in two hours to reposition the patient again
options.rationale: Scheduled repositioning limits the time any one area spends under pressure. Leaving now means any problem the turn created has two hours to develop.

questions.takeaway: Repositioning is not finished when the patient is moved. Alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and comfortable breathing are all reassessed afterward, because the turn is what put them at risk.

questions.stem: A critically ill patient with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome remains hypoxemic despite mechanical ventilation. The team plans to place the patient face down with the head turned to one side. Which statement explains this intervention?

options.text: It is a comfort measure that reduces pressure on the sacrum during long periods of bed rest
options.rationale: Turning a patient does relieve pressure on whatever area was bearing weight. Prone positioning is a respiratory intervention here, and treating it as a skin measure misses why the team is doing it.

options.text: It prevents contractures by holding the hips and shoulders in extension
options.rationale: Positioning does prevent contractures by carrying joints out of a fixed posture. It is a genuine goal of positioning in general and not the indication in this stem.

options.text: It is first-line therapy for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.rationale: Prone positioning means lying on the stomach with the head facing left or right. It is first-line therapy for patients who are critically ill with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, which is precisely the condition and severity described.

options.text: It allows easier access to the airway for suctioning and tube care
options.rationale: Access to the airway is a practical consideration during any position change. Less, which is one of the reasons proning requires a trained team.

questions.takeaway: Prone positioning is a treatment for the lungs, not a comfort or skin measure. Its stated indication is first-line therapy in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient has been confined to bed for two weeks. Which findings are consistent with the metabolic and psychosocial effects of immobility? Select all that apply.

options.text: Expressions of boredom and loss of independence
options.rationale: Psychosocial effects are the ways immobility changes how a patient feels and functions socially. They matter clinically because a patient who has stopped caring stops participating in the activity that would reverse the physical decline.

options.text: Increased metabolic demand with weight gain
options.rationale: Metabolic demand is the energy the body is using. The effect listed is reduced metabolic demand, so this option has the direction reversed.

options.text: Decreased appetite
options.rationale: Appetite is the drive to eat. It compounds the problem, because a patient already in negative nitrogen balance is taking in less of the protein needed to reverse it.

options.text: Improved sleep quality from increased rest
options.rationale: Rest and sleep are not the same thing. Patients confined to bed commonly sleep worse, and nothing in the effects of immobility predicts improvement.

options.text: Rising serum calcium with decreased bone density
options.rationale: Altered calcium metabolism is a listed metabolic effect, and bone demineralization is a musculoskeletal one. Bone releases mineral when nothing is stressing it, which is why weight bearing protects bone.

options.text: Loss of lean muscle mass
options.rationale: Lean muscle mass is the protein-containing tissue that does the work of movement. The body breaks down more than it takes in, a state called negative nitrogen balance, and the tissue lost is muscle.

questions.takeaway: Immobility reduces metabolic demand while producing negative nitrogen balance, altered calcium metabolism, loss of lean mass, and decreased appetite, alongside boredom, isolation, anxiety, depression, and altered self-concept.

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient reports a fall at home last month with no injury. Has lived alone since a spouse died two years ago and says most days are spent in a recliner watching television. Reports smoking about a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years and drinking three to four beers most evenings. Walks to the mailbox and back once a day without a device. Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement. Reports a serving of milk or yogurt on most days. Height has decreased by two inches over the past decade. Grip is symmetrical and strong bilaterally.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that place this patient at risk for further loss of musculoskeletal health.

segments.text: reports a fall at home last month with no injury
segments.rationale: A prior fall is the strongest single predictor of a future fall. The event demonstrates that balance or strength already failed once, and the next fall may land differently.

segments.text: most days are spent in a recliner watching television
segments.rationale: Sedentary time is time without load on muscle and bone. Sitting for most of the day supplies neither, and disuse takes muscle and bone apart.

segments.text: smoking about a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years
segments.rationale: Tobacco use is named among the things to avoid in order to maintain musculoskeletal health. Four decades, which is a sustained modifiable risk rather than an incidental one.

segments.text: drinking three to four beers most evenings
segments.rationale: Excessive alcohol is to be limited for musculoskeletal health. Yes, it is a daily pattern well above moderate intake, and alcohol also contributes to falls and to poor nutrition.

segments.text: Walks to the mailbox and back once a day without a device
segments.rationale: Independent ambulation without an assistive device is preserved function. It is something to build on rather than a risk.

segments.text: Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement
segments.rationale: Appropriate calcium and vitamin D intake is one of the listed measures that promotes musculoskeletal health. No, it describes the patient already doing one of the right things.

segments.text: Reports a serving of milk or yogurt on most days
segments.rationale: Adequate nutrition supports bone and muscle. Combined with the supplement, intake appears adequate.

segments.text: Height has decreased by two inches over the past decade
segments.rationale: Height loss reflects vertebral compression from reduced bone density. It signals osteopenia or osteoporosis, which is the aging change most likely to produce a fracture, and it is measurable evidence that bone has already been lost.

segments.text: Grip is symmetrical and strong bilaterally
segments.rationale: Symmetry and strength on bilateral comparison are normal findings. Comparing sides is how you establish that, and both sides are equal and strong.

questions.takeaway: Musculoskeletal health is promoted by regular physical activity, weight-bearing exercise, adequate nutrition, appropriate calcium and vitamin D, avoiding tobacco, and limiting excessive alcohol. Each of those is a place a patient can be losing ground.

questions.stem: A nurse positions a patient in supported Fowler's position. Which finding indicates the position is correct?

options.text: The legs are fully extended and flat against the mattress
options.rationale: Extension with no hip or knee flexion causes the patient to slide and shear.

options.text: The head is flexed forward onto the chest
options.rationale: Loses the normal cervical curve and restricts the airway.

options.text: The arms hang unsupported over the sides of the bed
options.rationale: Unsupported limbs pull on the shoulders and disturb alignment.

options.text: The hips and knees are flexed with the normal spinal curves maintained
options.rationale: Support must permit flexion of the hips and knees and preserve the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar curves.

questions.takeaway: Supported means the body is held in alignment, not merely propped up.

questions.stem: A patient on prolonged bed rest says the days feel pointless and has stopped asking to sit in the chair. Which nursing response best addresses this finding?

options.text: Arrange activities the patient values and involve family in the daily routine
options.rationale: Boredom, isolation, and loss of independence are listed psychosocial effects. They matter because a patient who disengages stops doing the activity that reverses the physical decline.

options.text: Explain that the rest is medically necessary and will end soon
options.rationale: Reassurance that closes the conversation and leaves the isolation unaddressed.

options.text: Document that the patient is depressed and notify the provider
options.rationale: Charting a label in place of acting. Nothing changes for the patient today.

options.text: Limit visitors so the patient can rest more fully
options.rationale: Increases isolation, which is the problem rather than the treatment.

questions.takeaway: Psychosocial effects are not the soft part of the list. They become physical decline.

questions.stem: A patient has been on bed rest for five days and has not had a bowel movement. Which mechanism explains this?

options.text: Increased metabolic demand consuming available fluid
options.rationale: Immobility lowers metabolic demand rather than raising it.

options.text: Decreased gastrointestinal motility from immobility
options.rationale: Immobility slows peristalsis, so stool moves less and water is reabsorbed from it.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance reducing stool bulk
options.rationale: Negative nitrogen balance describes protein breakdown and loss of lean mass, not bowel transit.

options.text: Bone demineralization altering calcium absorption
