options.rationale: The single most dangerous sick-day error. Insulin need usually rises during illness.

options.text: Wait until the fever settles before contacting the provider
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting, ketones, or a glucose that will not come down need reporting rather than waiting.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: never stop insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, test ketones above 240, and keep fluids going.
questions.strategy: Two options tell the patient to wait or to stop. Ask what illness does to the insulin requirement.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.detail: Stress hormones raise the glucose.
The need goes up, not down.
Vomiting with ketones is what needs reporting.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A patient using an insulin pump reports the glucose has risen from 140 to 310 mg/dL over four hours and ketones are now present. Which does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: A faulty glucose meter
options.rationale: The ketones corroborate the reading. Two findings agreeing is not a meter fault.

options.text: The pump is delivering too much basal insulin
options.rationale: Too much would lower the glucose, not raise it, and would not produce ketones.

options.text: An expected rise after a high-carbohydrate meal
options.rationale: A meal does not produce ketones, and the rise would not continue over four hours.

options.text: An interruption in insulin delivery at the site or in the tubing
options.rationale: A pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin, with no long-acting reserve. An occlusion or dislodged cannula leaves the patient with no insulin at all within hours.

questions.takeaway: Pump patients have no long-acting insulin on board. An interruption produces hyperglycemia and ketones within hours.
questions.strategy: Ask what a pump does and does not deliver. The ketones are the finding that rules out a simple meal-related rise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid-acting only, no basal reserve.
They indicate no insulin is reaching the patient.

steps.action: Cut the meal and meter options
steps.detail: Neither explains ketones.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an interruption in delivery.

skills.title: Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalances
skills.subtitle: Normal ranges, the findings each imbalance produces in both directions, ECG changes, and the rate limits to carry

questions.stem: A patient's serum sodium is 126 mEq/L. Which findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Headache, confusion, and lethargy
options.rationale: Low sodium means the outside of the cell is dilute, so water moves in and brain cells swell. Every serious finding in hyponatremia is a brain finding.

options.text: Dry, sticky mucous membranes and intense thirst
options.rationale: That is hypernatremia. Thirst and dry sticky membranes appear when the extracellular space is concentrated.

options.text: Muscle cramps and diminished deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Swelling affects muscle cells as well, producing cramps, generalized weakness, and reduced reflexes.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds with nausea and abdominal cramping
options.rationale: The gastrointestinal tract is one of the few systems that becomes more active in hyponatremia.

options.text: Seizures
options.rationale: As brain swelling progresses inside a skull that cannot expand, seizures and coma follow.

options.text: Flushed dry skin with a rising temperature
options.rationale: A hypernatremia finding, produced by water loss rather than water gain.

questions.takeaway: Hyponatremia is under 136 mEq/L. Water moves into cells and they swell, so the findings are neurologic first: headache, confusion, lethargy, then seizures. Add muscle cramps, weakness, reduced reflexes, and a hyperactive gut.
questions.strategy: Options B and F are both hypernatremia findings. Fixing the direction first, water in versus water out, sorts every option without memorizing two separate lists.

strategies: Set the direction before reading the options
Sort findings by which way water moved

steps.detail: Low sodium outside means water moves into the cell.
Swollen brain cells in a fixed skull.
Thirst, dry membranes, and flushed dry skin all belong to water loss.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient's serum potassium is 6.6 mEq/L. Which findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tall, peaked T waves on the monitor
options.rationale: The earliest and most important cardiac change, followed by a prolonged PR, flattened P waves, and a widening QRS.

options.text: Prominent U wave
options.rationale: A U wave belongs to hypokalemia. It is a wave appearing where there should be nothing.

options.text: Early tingling and muscle twitching, then flaccid paralysis
options.rationale: The cell sits closer to threshold and fires too easily, then stays depolarized and cannot reset.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds, diarrhea, and abdominal cramping
options.rationale: The gut speeds up, which is the mirror image of hypokalemia and a useful bedside discriminator.

options.text: Constipation with hypoactive bowel sounds
options.rationale: That is hypokalemia, where smooth muscle slows.

options.text: Bradycardia with a weak, irregular pulse
options.rationale: As conduction fails the rate falls, progressing toward heart block, ventricular fibrillation, or asystole.

questions.takeaway: Hyperkalemia is over 5.0 mEq/L. Cells depolarize too easily and then cannot reset. Cardiac changes come first and kill fastest: peaked T waves, prolonged PR, flat P waves, widened QRS, then a sine wave.
questions.strategy: Options B and E are hypokalemia findings. Potassium is the one electrolyte where low makes cells less excitable, so the two lists are true opposites and mixing them is the intended error.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Check the gut, which moves opposite between the two directions

steps.detail: High potassium means closer to threshold, then stuck.
Peaked T, not a U wave.
Faster, not slower.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: What is the normal range for serum potassium?

options.text: 1.3 to 2.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: That is the magnesium range.

options.text: 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L
options.rationale: Potassium runs 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L. The range is narrow because 98 percent of body potassium is inside cells, so the serum value represents a small remainder.

options.text: 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL
options.rationale: That is total serum calcium.

options.text: 136 to 145 mEq/L
options.rationale: That is sodium.

questions.takeaway: Sodium 136 to 145 mEq/L. Potassium 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L. Total calcium 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL. Magnesium 1.3 to 2.1 mEq/L. Phosphorus 3.0 to 4.5 mg/dL. Chloride 98 to 106 mEq/L.
questions.strategy: The distractors are the other four electrolyte ranges, so knowing the set matters more than knowing any one of them.

strategies: Learn the ranges as a set
Match the units to the electrolyte

steps.detail: Calcium and phosphorus are reported in mg/dL, the rest in mEq/L.
136 to 145 is far too high for potassium.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: Which electrocardiogram change is characteristic of hypokalemia?

options.text: Tall, peaked T waves
options.rationale: Peaked T waves are the hallmark of hyperkalemia.

options.text: Shortened ST segment and shortened QT interval
options.rationale: That combination belongs to hypercalcemia.

options.text: ST depression, flattened T wave, and a prominent U wave
options.rationale: The U wave is the signature of hypokalemia: a wave appearing where there should be nothing, alongside ST depression and a flattened or inverted T wave.

options.text: Prolonged PR interval with a widened QRS and bradycardia
options.rationale: That is hypermagnesemia.

questions.takeaway: Potassium moves the T wave: flattened when low, peaked when high, and only the low side adds a U wave. Calcium and magnesium move the QT interval in opposite directions depending on which way the level went.
questions.strategy: All four options are real tracings from real imbalances, so this is a matching task rather than a reasoning one. Anchor on the U wave, which appears in only one place.

strategies: Anchor on the finding unique to one imbalance
Group the tracings by electrolyte

steps.detail: A U wave occurs only in hypokalemia.
Peaked T to high potassium, short QT to high calcium.
Prolonged PR with wide QRS to high magnesium.

elimination.verdict: C is correct.

questions.stem: A patient's total serum calcium is 7.6 mg/dL. Which findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips
options.rationale: Perioral and fingertip paresthesia is the earliest finding, because calcium no longer blocks sodium channels and nerves fire on their own.

options.text: Carpal spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic
options.rationale: A positive Trousseau sign, produced by the same nerve irritability.

options.text: Profound muscle weakness with absent deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: That is hypercalcemia. Low calcium produces hyperactive reflexes, not absent ones.

options.text: Prolonged ST segment and prolonged QT interval
options.rationale: The cardiac signature of hypocalcemia, which can deteriorate into torsades de pointes.

options.text: Constipation with hypoactive bowel sounds
options.rationale: Also hypercalcemia. Low calcium produces hyperactive bowel sounds and diarrhea.

options.text: Laryngospasm and stridor
options.rationale: Tetany of the larynx. It closes the airway without warning and is the reason emergency airway equipment stays at the bedside after neck surgery.

questions.takeaway: Hypocalcemia is under 9.0 mg/dL total. Calcium stabilizes the nerve membrane, so losing it makes everything overexcitable: tingling, twitching, tetany, Trousseau, Chvostek, a long QT, and at the extreme laryngospasm and seizures.
questions.strategy: Options C and E are the hypercalcemia picture. Low means overexcitable and high means underexcitable, and that single rule sorts calcium and magnesium in both directions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Apply the excitability rule to the direction given

steps.detail: Low calcium equals more excitable.
Firing nerves: tingling, spasm, tetany.
Absent reflexes and constipation are the high-calcium picture.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: What is the maximum rate at which IV potassium chloride may be infused?

options.text: 5 mEq per hour, and only through a central line
options.rationale: Understates the limit and adds a central line requirement that does not exist. Diluted potassium runs peripherally within concentration limits.

options.text: 40 mEq per hour with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Double the maximum. Monitoring does not make an unsafe rate safe.

options.text: There is no maximum as long as the solution is diluted
options.rationale: Dilution addresses vein irritation. The rate limit exists because a rapid potassium load stops the heart.

options.text: 10 to 20 mEq per hour, with cardiac monitoring above 10 mEq per hour
options.rationale: The standard limit. Peripheral concentration is about 1 mEq per 10 mL, and urine output must be at least 30 mL per hour before administration.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium runs at 10 to 20 mEq per hour maximum, never as a push or bolus, always diluted and on a pump, at about 1 mEq per 10 mL peripherally, and only when urine output is at least 30 mL per hour. Rates above 10 mEq per hour require continuous cardiac monitoring.
questions.strategy: Option B is the number most often seen on an incorrect prescription, which is exactly why it appears as a distractor.

strategies: Know the limit as a number, not a feeling
Reject options that substitute monitoring for a safe rate

steps.detail: 10 to 20 mEq per hour.
40 exceeds it regardless of monitoring.
Potassium has a rate limit in every setting.

elimination.verdict: D is correct.

questions.stem: Disappearing deep tendon reflexes are the earliest reliable sign of which electrolyte imbalance?

options.text: Hypermagnesemia
options.rationale: Magnesium suppresses in a predictable order: reflexes go first, then blood pressure and heart rate, then consciousness, then breathing. That order is why reflexes are checked on a schedule during any magnesium infusion.

options.text: Hypomagnesemia
options.rationale: Low magnesium produces hyperactive reflexes, tremor, and tetany, the same overexcitable picture as low calcium.

options.text: Hypocalcemia
options.rationale: Low calcium also produces hyperactive reflexes, along with Trousseau and Chvostek signs.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: Low potassium produces diminished reflexes as part of ascending weakness, but the earliest finding is leg weakness rather than reflex loss, and it is not the monitored parameter.

questions.takeaway: During a magnesium sulfate infusion, hold for an absent patellar reflex, a respiratory rate under 12, or urine output under 30 mL per hour. Calcium gluconate is the antidote and stays at the bedside.
questions.strategy: Options B and C are the overexcitable mirror image. High magnesium shuts firing down; low magnesium and low calcium turn it up.

strategies: Apply the excitability rule
Recall which parameter is monitored during an infusion

steps.detail: High magnesium means less excitable.
Low magnesium and low calcium both produce hyperactive reflexes.
Reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output are the hold parameters.

elimination.verdict: A is correct.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate fluid volume deficit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tachycardia with a thready, weak pulse
options.rationale: The heart speeds up before the pressure falls, which is why a normal blood pressure does not rule out a deficit.

options.text: Urine output under 30 mL per hour with a specific gravity above 1.030
options.rationale: The kidney concentrates urine to hold water. Dark, concentrated, low-volume urine is the renal signature.

options.text: Distended neck veins and an S3 gallop
options.rationale: Both are fluid volume excess findings. In a deficit the neck veins are flat when the patient is supine.

options.text: Rising hematocrit, hemoglobin, and BUN
options.rationale: Hemoconcentration. The solutes stayed and the water left, so the values rise without anything being gained.

options.text: Crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: Crackles indicate fluid crossing into the alveoli, which is overload rather than deficit.

options.text: Orthostatic drop of 20 mm Hg systolic on standing
options.rationale: Lost vascular volume cannot maintain pressure against gravity. This is also why these patients fall.

questions.takeaway: Fluid volume deficit: tachycardia first and hypotension late, flat neck veins, urine under 30 mL per hour with high specific gravity, dry membranes, poor turgor at the sternum, and hemoconcentration. One liter lost is one kilogram, or 2.2 pounds.
questions.strategy: Options C and E are the overload picture. Sorting by whether the vascular space is too full or too empty assigns every finding without memorizing two lists.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Ask whether the vessels are full or empty

steps.detail: Deficit means the vascular space is empty.
Fast, thready, flat neck veins, concentrated urine.
Distended veins, an S3, and crackles all mean too much.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: In hypernatremia, what happens at the cellular level?

options.text: Water moves into cells and they swell
options.rationale: That is hyponatremia. Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, which in hyponatremia is inside the cell.

options.text: Water moves out of cells and they shrink
options.rationale: The extracellular space is concentrated, so water is pulled out. Shrinking brain cells produce agitation and restlessness first, then lethargy and seizures.

options.text: Sodium moves into cells, raising the intracellular sodium
options.rationale: Sodium is kept out of cells by the sodium-potassium pump. The imbalance moves water, not sodium.

options.text: Potassium moves out of cells to compensate
options.rationale: Potassium shifts in response to pH and insulin, not to a sodium concentration change.

questions.takeaway: Sodium is the cation that holds water in the extracellular space, so the serum sodium tells you which direction water is moving across every cell membrane. High sodium pulls water out and cells shrink; low sodium pushes water in and cells swell.
questions.strategy: Option A is the same mechanism in reverse and is chosen whenever the direction is not fixed before reading the options.

strategies: Fix the direction first
Remember that water moves, not sodium

steps.detail: High serum sodium means the outside is concentrated.
Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, so out of the cell.
The imbalance moves water.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: Using ROME, a pH of 7.28 with a PaCO2 of 55 mm Hg indicates which imbalance?

options.text: Metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: In a metabolic problem the pH and the bicarbonate move in the same direction. Here the abnormal value given is the carbon dioxide.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: The pH is 7.28, which is acidotic. Alkalosis requires a pH above 7.45.

options.text: Respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Respiratory Opposite: the pH is low and the carbon dioxide is high, moving in opposite directions, so the lungs are the cause.

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis shows a high pH with a low carbon dioxide, which is the same relationship running the other way.

questions.takeaway: ROME: Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal. Read the pH, then the carbon dioxide against 35 to 45, then the bicarbonate against 21 to 28, then decide the compensation. Normal pH with both other values abnormal is full compensation.
questions.strategy: Half the options are eliminated by the pH alone, since 7.28 is acidotic. The carbon dioxide then decides respiratory versus metabolic.

strategies: Read the pH before anything else
Apply ROME to the second value

steps.detail: 7.28 is acidosis, so both alkalosis options are out.
55 is high, opposite the low pH.
Opposite directions means respiratory.

elimination.verdict: C is correct.

skills.title: Infusion Therapy
skills.subtitle: Device thresholds, tonicity, infiltration versus phlebitis, dwell times, calculations, and emergency positioning

questions.stem: Above what osmolarity must an IV solution be given through a central line?

options.text: 300 mOsm/L
options.rationale: Close to the osmolarity of normal saline at 308 mOsm/L, which infuses peripherally without difficulty.

options.text: 450 mOsm/L
options.rationale: Below the threshold. Several routine peripheral solutions sit in this range, including 5 percent dextrose in 0.45 percent saline at 406 mOsm/L.

options.text: 600 mOsm/L
options.rationale: Above 600 mOsm/L the solution pulls water out of the cells lining the vein and damages it, so it requires the rapid dilution that central circulation provides.

options.text: 900 mOsm/L
options.rationale: Too high. Damage occurs well before this, which is why the accepted threshold is 600.

questions.takeaway: Four facts choose the device: a pH below 5 or above 9, an osmolarity above 600 mOsm/L, any vesicant, or a course longer than about two weeks. Parenteral nutrition runs above 1,400 mOsm/L and must never go peripherally.
questions.strategy: Every option is a plausible round number. The threshold is worth memorizing as a fact, because it appears in prescription-questioning items constantly.

strategies: Memorize the four device thresholds as a set
Anchor to a known solution

steps.detail: Normal saline is 308 and runs peripherally.
600 mOsm/L is the peripheral ceiling.
Parenteral nutrition at 1,400 is far above it.

elimination.verdict: C is correct.

questions.stem: Which pH range allows a medication to be given through a peripheral IV?

options.text: 5 to 9
options.rationale: Below 5 or above 9 strips the endothelial lining of a small vein. Amiodarone, vancomycin, and ciprofloxacin all sit below pH 5 and cause phlebitis on a long peripheral course.

options.text: 3 to 11
options.rationale: Far too wide. A pH of 3 is strongly acidic and destroys a peripheral vein.
Narrower than the actual limit. Many routine peripheral solutions fall outside this and are given safely.

options.text: 4 to 10
options.rationale: Close to the real range and wrong at both ends. The accepted limits are 5 and 9.

questions.takeaway: A pH below 5 or above 9 requires central access, as does an osmolarity above 600 mOsm/L, any vesicant, and a therapy running longer than about two weeks.
questions.strategy: Option D is the near-miss, one point off at each end. Ranges are tested this way, so the exact numbers matter more than the concept.

strategies: Learn thresholds as exact numbers
Watch for a range that is off by one at each end

steps.detail: 5 and 9.
3 to 11 would allow strongly acidic drugs.
4 to 10 is the same idea with wrong endpoints.

elimination.verdict: A is correct.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate infiltration at a peripheral IV site? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skin that is cool to the touch
options.rationale: Room-temperature fluid is pooling in tissue that is not inflamed, so the area runs cool. Temperature is the discriminator between infiltration and phlebitis.

options.text: A red streak following the line of the vein
options.rationale: A streak follows the vein, which makes it phlebitis. Infiltration spreads around the site instead.

options.text: Taut, blanched, swollen skin
options.rationale: Fluid accumulating in the tissue stretches the skin and blanches it.

options.text: A palpable cord along the vein
options.rationale: A palpable venous cord is a phlebitis finding and part of its grade 3 definition.

options.text: The infusion slowing or stopping
options.rationale: Tissue pressure rises around the catheter tip and resists the flow.

options.text: Burning or tenderness at the site
options.rationale: Discomfort increases as the volume in the tissue grows.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration runs cool and spreads around the site. Phlebitis runs warm and follows the vein. Stop the infusion first in either case, and never apply pressure to an infiltration, which forces solution into more tissue.
questions.strategy: Options B and D are both phlebitis findings and both describe something following the vein. Where the findings are located separates the two as reliably as temperature does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Use temperature and location to separate the two

steps.detail: Fluid in tissue, not an inflamed vein.
Cool, because nothing is inflamed.
Streaks and cords are phlebitis.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate phlebitis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warmth along the vein
options.rationale: The vein wall itself is inflamed, so the area runs warm rather than cool.

options.text: Blanched, cool skin around the site
options.rationale: That is infiltration. Phlebitis does not blanch and does not run cool.

options.text: Redness following the path of the vein
options.rationale: Findings track the vein rather than spreading around the insertion point.

options.text: A firm, palpable cord
options.rationale: The inflamed vein becomes thickened and can be felt as a cord. A cord over one inch with purulent drainage is grade 4.

options.text: Tenderness or pain at the site
options.rationale: Pain with erythema is grade 2 and is present through the higher grades.

options.text: Gross edema more than 6 inches from the site
options.rationale: Extensive edema is how infiltration is graded, not phlebitis.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis grades from 0 to 4: erythema alone, then pain with erythema or edema, then streak formation with a palpable cord, then a cord over one inch with purulent drainage. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, warm compress, elevate, and document the grade.
questions.strategy: Options B and F are the infiltration picture. The two complications share swelling and pain, so the distinguishing features are temperature, direction, and whether a cord is present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Ask whether the finding follows the vein

steps.detail: The vein wall is inflamed.
Warm.
Blanching, coolness, and gross edema.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: What is the smallest catheter gauge generally used to transfuse blood in an adult?

options.text: 24 gauge
options.rationale: Too narrow for an adult transfusion. It is preferred for infants, small children, and fragile veins.

options.text: 22 gauge
options.rationale: Blood can infuse through a 22 gauge without damaging the cells, and policies commonly prefer a 20 gauge while setting 22 as the smallest acceptable in an adult.

options.text: 18 gauge
options.rationale: Adequate and larger than required. Preferred for surgery, where rapid volume is the goal.

options.text: 16 gauge
options.rationale: Reserved for trauma and rapid fluid resuscitation. Larger catheters fill more of the vein and cause phlebitis more often.

questions.takeaway: Choose the smallest gauge that will deliver the therapy. Blood in an adult usually goes through a 20 gauge, and never smaller than a 22, because a narrower lumen shears red cells. Larger gauges flow faster and cause phlebitis more often.
questions.strategy: The instinct is that bigger is safer for blood, which makes 18 and 16 attractive. The rule runs the other way: the smallest gauge that does the job.

strategies: Ask for the smallest adequate size, not the largest
Separate the preferred size from the minimum

steps.detail: Smallest gauge that delivers the therapy.
Never smaller than 22 in an adult.
18 and 16 are for rapid resuscitation.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: Which formula calculates a gravity drip rate in drops per minute?

options.text: Total volume in mL divided by total time in hours
options.rationale: That gives the pump rate in mL per hour, not drops per minute.

options.text: Total volume in mL times the drop factor, divided by time in minutes
options.rationale: Volume times drop factor divided by minutes. Convert hours to minutes first, and round the result to a whole drop.

options.text: Drop factor divided by total volume, times time in hours
options.rationale: Inverts the relationship. A larger volume would produce a slower rate, which is backward.

options.text: Total volume in mL divided by the drop factor, times time in minutes
options.rationale: Divides by the drop factor instead of multiplying, so a larger drop factor would lower the rate.

questions.takeaway: Drops per minute equals total volume in mL times the drop factor, divided by time in minutes. Macrodrip sets deliver 10, 15, or 20 gtt/mL and state it on the package. Microdrip is always 60 gtt/mL, and with microdrip the drops per minute equal the mL per hour.
questions.strategy: Check the direction of each formula against common sense: a bigger drop factor means more drops for the same volume, so it must multiply rather than divide.

strategies: Test each formula against what should happen
Check that the units cancel

steps.detail: Volume over hours gives mL per hour.
More drops per mL must increase the rate, so it multiplies.
Time in minutes belongs in the denominator.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: How often is blood administration tubing changed?

options.text: Every 24 hours
options.rationale: That is the interval for intermittent sets and for parenteral nutrition tubing.

options.text: Every 96 hours
options.rationale: That is the minimum interval for a continuous administration set.

options.text: Every 7 days
options.rationale: That is the maximum interval for a continuous set and the usual interval for a transparent dressing.

options.text: Every 4 hours or every 2 units
options.rationale: Blood is a growth medium, so the interval is short and is a hard limit rather than a guideline.

questions.takeaway: Blood set every 4 hours or 2 units. Intermittent and parenteral nutrition sets every 24 hours. Continuous sets no more often than every 96 hours and at least every 7 days. Transparent dressing every 5 to 7 days, gauze every 2 days, and any dressing at once if damp, loose, or soiled.
questions.strategy: All four options are real intervals from this same list, so the question is whether the intervals are learned as a set attached to what each one covers.

strategies: Learn the intervals as one table
Match the interval to the infection risk

steps.detail: Blood supports growth faster than anything else on the list.
4 hours or 2 units.
24 hours intermittent, 96 hours to 7 days continuous.

elimination.verdict: D is correct.

questions.stem: Which elements are part of the central line insertion bundle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hand hygiene
options.rationale: The foundation of the bundle and of every step within it.

options.text: Maximal sterile barrier precautions
options.rationale: The patient draped head to toe, the inserter in sterile gloves, gown, and mask, and everyone in the room masked.

options.text: Chlorhexidine skin antisepsis allowed to dry
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine in alcohol applied with friction and allowed to dry, because drying time is when it works.

options.text: Femoral vein preferred in adults
options.rationale: The femoral site is avoided in adults and chosen last. Upper arm and subclavian come first, then internal jugular.

options.text: Daily review of whether the line is still needed
options.rationale: The step that prevents more infections than any other, because risk rises with every day the device remains in place.

options.text: Scheduled catheter replacement every 7 days
options.rationale: Routine scheduled replacement does not reduce infection and is not part of the bundle. Removing the line when it is no longer needed does.

questions.takeaway: The central line bundle is hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers, chlorhexidine antisepsis, avoiding the femoral vein in adults, controlled insertion conditions, and a daily review of continued need.
questions.strategy: Options D and F are real practices stated backward. Femoral is the last site rather than the first, and scheduled replacement was abandoned in favor of removal when no longer needed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Watch for a real practice inverted

steps.detail: Hygiene, barriers, and antisepsis are all in.
Femoral is last in adults.
Daily review of need, not scheduled replacement.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: In which position is a patient placed when an air embolism is suspected?

options.text: High Fowler with the legs dependent
options.rationale: Upright positioning is correct for circulatory overload and harmful here, because it lets air travel toward the brain.

options.text: Right lateral with the head of the bed raised
options.rationale: Both the side and the head position are wrong. Air would move toward the pulmonary outflow tract.

options.text: Supine and flat
options.rationale: Flat alone does not trap the air. The left lateral component is what holds it in the right ventricle.

options.text: Left lateral with the head of the bed lowered
options.rationale: Left side with the head down traps air in the right ventricle, away from the pulmonary outflow tract, while oxygen is given and the emergency team is called.

questions.takeaway: Sudden dyspnea, cough, chest pain, hypotension, and tachycardia during a central line procedure is an air embolism. Clamp or cover the leak, place the patient left lateral with the head down, give oxygen, and call for emergency help.
questions.strategy: Option A is the default position for a breathless patient and is the wrong answer here, which is what makes this worth memorizing as a fact rather than reasoning toward.

strategies: Memorize the position rather than deriving it
Note where the air needs to stay

steps.detail: It enters the right side of the heart.
Left side keeps it away from the pulmonary outflow tract.
Prevents travel toward the brain.

elimination.verdict: D is correct.

questions.stem: Which solution is isotonic in the bag but acts hypotonic in the body?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Isotonic in the bag and isotonic in the body. It expands extracellular volume and does not enter cells.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Isotonic in both. It contains calcium, so it is held in hypercalcemia and never hung with blood.

options.text: 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: 272 mOsm/L in the bag, and the dextrose is metabolized within minutes, leaving free water. That is why it is never used to prime or flush blood tubing.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypotonic in the bag at 154 mOsm/L and hypotonic in the body. It never changes category.

questions.takeaway: Tonicity is stated for the moment of administration. Glucose is metabolized within minutes, so any dextrose solution acts more dilute in the body than the label reads. Only 0.9 percent sodium chloride goes with blood.
questions.strategy: The question depends entirely on knowing that dextrose disappears. Options A, B, and D all keep their category, so identifying the one containing dextrose answers it.

strategies: Find the solution that changes category
Ask what happens to the solute

steps.detail: Only one option contains it.
It is metabolized, leaving free water.
Saline and lactated Ringer's do not change.

elimination.verdict: C is correct.

skills.title: Mobility and Safe Patient Handling
skills.subtitle: Mobility criteria, immobility complications, range of motion, assistive devices, positioning, restraints, and delegation

questions.stem: On which side is a cane held?

options.text: The weaker side, to support it directly
options.rationale: Placing the cane on the weak side puts an unstable point under the leg least able to correct, and leaves the strong side with nothing to push against.

options.text: The stronger side, advanced with the weaker leg
options.rationale: The cane goes on the strong side and moves together with the weak leg, so support arrives at the moment the weak leg takes weight.

options.text: The stronger side, advanced with the stronger leg
options.rationale: The correct side with the wrong timing. The weak leg would step unsupported.

options.text: Either side, whichever the patient prefers
options.rationale: Cane placement is determined by which side is weaker, not by preference.

questions.takeaway: A cane is held on the stronger side and advanced together with the weaker leg, then the stronger leg follows. The handle sits at hip height with the elbow flexed about 15 to 30 degrees.
questions.strategy: Almost everyone answers the affected side first, because supporting the weak side sounds right. The cane substitutes for the weak leg rather than propping it up.

strategies: Settle the side before the timing
Ask what the device replaces

steps.detail: Strong side, because that is where the push comes from.
A is out on side alone.
Cane and weak leg move together.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: What must a patient do to pass a level of the mobility assessment?

options.text: Complete the task without becoming tachycardic, diaphoretic, or light-headed
options.rationale: Tolerance is the criterion. Cognition counts as well, because a patient who cannot follow the instruction cannot do the task safely.

options.text: Complete the task, regardless of how they tolerate it
options.rationale: Completion is not the standard. A patient can finish the movement and still be unsafe to advance.

options.text: Complete the task within a set time limit
options.rationale: There is no timed component. Speed is not what the assessment measures.

options.text: Complete the task without using any assistive device
options.rationale: Devices are matched to the level reached. Using one is the expected outcome, not a failure.

questions.takeaway: Mobility is assessed on admission, once a shift, and after any significant change. A patient advances only by passing each level, and the criterion at every level is completing the task without becoming tachycardic, diaphoretic, or light-headed.
questions.strategy: Option B is the intended error. It is what most people assume the assessment measures, and it is exactly the thing the criterion excludes.

strategies: Separate completing from tolerating
Recall that cognition is part of the criterion

steps.detail: Tolerance, not completion.
A patient can finish and still be unsafe.
Neither is part of the standard.

elimination.verdict: A is correct.

questions.stem: Which complications result from prolonged immobility? Select all that apply.

options.text: Atelectasis and hypostatic pneumonia
options.rationale: Shallow breathing and pooled secretions in a supine patient. Reduced chest expansion lowers tidal volume before anything sounds abnormal.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension
options.rationale: Vascular tone is lost, so the vessels no longer constrict on standing. This is what causes the fall at the moment of rising.

options.text: Increased bone density from rest
options.rationale: The opposite. Without weight-bearing, bone releases calcium it is no longer asked to hold, producing disuse osteoporosis and sometimes a raised serum calcium.

options.text: Renal calculi
options.rationale: The renal pelvis does not drain by gravity in a supine patient, and stasis plus the calcium released from bone forms stones.

options.text: Increased peristalsis and diarrhea
options.rationale: Peristalsis slows, producing constipation and at the extreme fecal impaction.

options.text: Pressure injury
options.rationale: Bone presses tissue against a surface, worsened by shear when the head of the bed is raised and the body slides down.

questions.takeaway: Immobility costs about 3 percent of muscle strength per day. Within days it produces atelectasis, thrombosis, and pressure injury; within weeks contracture and bone loss; and in older adults it is an independent risk factor for delirium.
questions.strategy: Options C and E are each the real effect reversed. Immobility slows or removes function; it does not improve anything, which makes any option describing a benefit of rest suspect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Reject any option describing a benefit of immobility

steps.detail: Immobility subtracts function.
Bone loses density without weight-bearing.
Slower, so constipation rather than diarrhea.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: How does a patient with a weak right leg use crutches on stairs?

options.text: Up with the right leg, down with the left leg
options.rationale: Reverses the rule in both directions. The weak leg would lead going up, taking full weight at the hardest point.

options.text: Up with the left leg, down with the crutches and the right leg
options.rationale: Up with the good leg, down with the bad. The strong leg lifts the body to the higher step; going down, the crutches and the weak leg descend first.

options.text: Up with the crutches first, down with the left leg
options.rationale: Crutches lead only on the way down. Leading with them going up leaves the patient unsupported mid-step.

options.text: Both legs together in each direction
options.rationale: Stairs are taken one leg at a time with crutches. Moving both at once removes the support the sequence depends on.

questions.takeaway: Up with the good leg first, down with the crutches and the bad leg first. Weight is carried through the hands and arms, never the axillae, with two to three finger widths of clearance under the arm.
questions.strategy: The rule is almost always tested by offering it reversed. Memorizing up with the good, down with the bad settles both directions at once.

strategies: Recall the rule before reading the options
Check both directions in each option

steps.detail: Up with the good, down with the bad.
The left, since the right is weak.
Up with the left, down with the crutches and the right.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: Which findings during ambulation mean the nurse stops the activity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Diaphoresis
options.rationale: Sweating during light activity signals the effort has exceeded what the patient can tolerate.

options.text: A heart rate rise of 8 beats per minute that settles with rest
options.rationale: A modest rise that recovers is a normal response to activity, not a reason to stop.

options.text: Dizziness or light-headedness
options.rationale: Signals inadequate cerebral perfusion and precedes a fall.

options.text: A drop in systolic blood pressure during the activity
options.rationale: Blood pressure should hold or rise with activity. Any fall means the cardiovascular system is not keeping up.

options.text: Pallor
options.rationale: Reduced peripheral perfusion, and one of the earliest visible signs that the activity is too much.

options.text: Mild fatigue that resolves within a minute of sitting
options.rationale: Expected with reconditioning after illness and not a stopping point.

questions.takeaway: Stop for dyspnea, chest pain, diaphoresis, pallor, or dizziness. A heart rate rise of more than about 20 beats per minute that does not recover, or any drop in systolic pressure during activity, means the activity exceeded what the patient could do today.
questions.strategy: Options B and F are both normal responses. The distinguishing feature is recovery: a change that settles with brief rest is tolerance, and one that does not is intolerance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Ask whether the change recovers

steps.detail: Some rise in heart rate and some fatigue are expected.
Settles quickly means tolerated.
Pallor, diaphoresis, dizziness, and a falling pressure.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: What does passive range of motion accomplish?

options.text: Builds muscle strength
options.rationale: Strength requires the patient's own muscles to contract. In passive movement the nurse does the work.

options.text: Improves cardiovascular endurance
options.rationale: Endurance requires sustained active effort, which passive movement does not provide.

options.text: Prevents joint contracture
options.rationale: Moving the joint through its range prevents the connective tissue shortening that produces a contracture. It preserves flexibility and builds nothing.

options.text: Increases muscle mass
options.rationale: Mass requires active contraction against resistance.

questions.takeaway: The question that sorts every type of movement is whether the muscle is contracting. If it is not, no strength is being built, only flexibility preserved. Active range of motion builds both; active-assist keeps what strength exists; passive prevents contracture only.
questions.strategy: Three options describe gains that require the patient to do the work. Passive means the nurse does it, which removes all three at once.

strategies: Ask who is doing the work
Match the outcome to the mechanism

steps.detail: The nurse moves the joint; the patient does not contract.
No contraction, so no strength, mass, or endurance.
Contracture prevention.

elimination.verdict: C is correct.

questions.stem: Which position is preferred for preventing pressure injury when turning a patient?

options.text: Full 90-degree side-lying
options.rationale: Places body weight directly over the trochanter, one of the highest-risk bony prominences.

options.text: Supine with the head of the bed at 60 degrees
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed causes the body to slide, and shear damages tissue at the sacrum more readily than pressure alone.

options.text: Prone with a pillow under the abdomen
options.rationale: Relieves the sacrum but is poorly tolerated and contraindicated with spinal, cardiac, and respiratory problems, so it is not the general answer.

options.text: Thirty-degree lateral with pillow support
options.rationale: Keeps weight off the trochanter and off the sacrum at the same time, which is why it is the preferred turning position.

questions.takeaway: The 30-degree lateral position is preferred for pressure injury prevention. Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or less when the condition allows, lift rather than drag using a slide sheet, and inspect bony prominences every shift.
questions.strategy: Option A is the usual mental image of turning a patient. The degree is the point of the question, and it exists specifically to avoid the trochanter.

strategies: Ask which bony prominence each position loads
Notice when a number is the answer

steps.detail: Loads the trochanter.
Adds shear at the sacrum.
Off both.

elimination.verdict: D is correct.

questions.stem: Which tasks may be delegated to assistive personnel? Select all that apply.

options.text: Measuring and recording intake and output
options.rationale: A measurement carried out against an established plan, with results reported to the nurse.

options.text: Assisting with ambulation according to an established plan
options.rationale: Within the role when the plan already exists and the direction names the device, the assistance needed, and what to report.

options.text: Deciding whether a patient is steady enough to walk today
options.rationale: That is an assessment. Deciding the mobility level always stays with the nurse.

options.text: Obtaining vital signs on a stable patient
options.rationale: Routine measurement on a patient whose condition is not changing.

options.text: Evaluating whether the fall prevention plan is working
options.rationale: Evaluation is a nursing responsibility. Assistive personnel report observations; they do not interpret them.

options.text: Repositioning and assisting with hygiene
options.rationale: Direct care carried out according to a schedule the nurse set.

questions.takeaway: The nurse assesses, decides, teaches, and evaluates. Assistive personnel carry out a plan someone else made and report what they observe. Delegating the task never delegates the outcome, and it never delegates the judgment about whether the patient can do it today.
questions.strategy: Options C and E are the two verbs that never move: deciding and evaluating. Scanning the options for those verbs answers most delegation questions without knowing the specific task.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Scan for the verbs that never delegate

steps.detail: Deciding steadiness is an assessment.
Judging whether a plan works is evaluation.
Measuring, assisting per plan, and direct care all delegate.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: To what is a limb restraint secured?

options.text: The side rail, so it moves with the rail
options.rationale: A rail that is raised or lowered tightens the restraint and can injure the patient. Restraints are never tied to a side rail.

options.text: The movable part of the bed frame
options.rationale: The frame moves with the bed, so raising or lowering the bed does not change the tension on the restraint.

options.text: The headboard
options.rationale: The headboard is usually fixed and does not move with the bed, so position changes alter the tension.

options.text: The mattress itself
options.rationale: A mattress shifts within the frame, so a restraint anchored to it provides no reliable tension or security.

questions.takeaway: A restraint is the last option after documented alternatives, requires a time-limited prescription that is never written as needed, uses the least restrictive type, is tied with a quick-release knot to the movable bed frame, and is monitored every 15 to 30 minutes with release and care every 2 hours.
questions.strategy: Option A is the single most common wrong answer and the reason the rule exists. It is also the error most often observed in practice.

strategies: Ask what happens when the bed moves
Recall the rule as an absolute

steps.detail: A moving rail changes the tension.
Headboard and mattress do not track the bed.
Tension stays constant.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A muscle strength grade of 3 out of 5 indicates what ability?

options.text: Movement against gravity but not against resistance
options.rationale: Grade 3 lifts the limb against gravity and cannot hold it against any added resistance. Grade 4 tolerates some resistance and grade 5 is normal.

options.text: Movement only when gravity is eliminated
options.rationale: That is grade 2, where the limb moves along a surface but cannot lift against gravity.

options.text: A flicker of contraction with no movement
options.rationale: That is grade 1. Grade 0 is no contraction at all.

options.text: Full strength against full resistance
options.rationale: That is grade 5, normal strength.

questions.takeaway: Muscle strength grades 0 to 5: 0 no contraction, 1 a flicker, 2 movement with gravity eliminated, 3 movement against gravity, 4 movement against some resistance, 5 normal. A difference between sides matters more than the absolute grade.
questions.strategy: The scale is learned as a whole or not at all, since every distractor is another grade on the same scale.

strategies: Learn the scale as a sequence
Anchor at the ends and count inward

steps.detail: 0 is nothing, 5 is normal.
Grade 2 cannot beat gravity, grade 3 can.
Resistance begins at grade 4.

elimination.verdict: A is correct.
